statement: Yamazaki found that British Columbia's carbon tax generated a small but statistically significant 0.74 percent annual increase in employment over 2007-2013, while the most carbon-intensive and trade-sensitive industries lost jobs.
anchor: By aggregating across industries I find the BC carbon tax generated, on average, a small but statistically significant 0.74 percent annual increases in employment over the 2007-2013 period.
the most carbon-intensive and trade-sensitive industries see employment fall with the tax, while clean service industries see employment rise.
context: Peer-reviewed single-author study (Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 2017, University of Calgary). Author calls it "initial evidence"; the result depends on revenue recycling through tax cuts. The author's other work is not independent of it.

statement: Metcalf's regressions associate a $30 carbon tax with roughly a 6 percent increase in British Columbia's GDP, but he cautions that the estimates are imprecise and concludes only that GDP has not been adversely affected.
anchor: A $30 carbon tax is associated with a roughly 6 percent increase in GDP.
Given the imprecise estimates, we should not lean too heavily on these results.
But it seems fair to say that GDP has not been adversely affected by the carbon tax.
context: Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, 2019, by Gilbert Metcalf (Tufts). The Table 5 tax-rate coefficients are not statistically significant, as the paper itself notes. Metcalf later co-authored Metcalf and Stock (2023), so those two are not independent of each other.

statement: British Columbia cancelled its consumer carbon tax by dropping the rate to $0 effective April 1, 2025, taking approximately 17 cents per litre off the cost of fuel and approximately 15 cents per cubic metre off natural gas.
anchor: The B.C. government is cancelling the carbon tax by introducing legislation to drop the rate to $0, effective Tuesday, April 1, 2025.
taking approximately 17 cents per litre off the cost of fuel and approximately 15 cents per cubic metre for natural gas on their home heating bill.
context: Province of British Columbia release, 2025-03-31, NDP government under Premier David Eby. The province said it was aligning with the end of the federal consumer fuel charge; it gave no emissions forecast for the repeal. Industrial carbon pricing stays in place.

statement: The B.C. government estimated that cancelling the carbon tax and the climate action tax credit would have an impact of $1.99 billion in the coming fiscal year, and that families would otherwise have paid approximately $410 in 2025-26.
anchor: Cancelling the tax and the credit will have an estimated impact of $1.99 billion in the coming fiscal year.
The average amount of carbon tax that would have been paid by families in B.C. is approximately $410 in 2025-26.
context: Province of British Columbia estimates (Ministry of Finance, 2025-03-31). The tax credit was cancelled with the tax, so the $1.99 billion is net of lost credit payments only as the province states it.

statement: Under the Government of Canada's 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan, the federal fuel charge was set to rise from $65 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023-24 to $170 per tonne in 2030-31.
anchor: Under the Government’s 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan, the federal fuel charge is set to rise from $65 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023-24 to $170 per tonne in 2030-31.
context: PBO (non-partisan officer of Parliament), 2023-03-30. This was the schedule under the Trudeau government; it ended with the April 2025 zero rate. The fuel charge applied only in provinces without their own system (backstop provinces).

statement: The Government of Canada made regulations setting all federal fuel charge rates to zero from April 1, 2025, while saying a price on pollution for large emitters would continue.
anchor: The Government of Canada has made regulations that cease the application of the federal fuel charge, effective April 1, 2025, and is also removing requirements for provinces and territories to have a consumer-facing carbon price as of that date.
After March 31, 2025, the applicable fuel charge rates for all types of fuel and for combustible waste will be set to zero.
A price on pollution for large emitters will continue to be a pillar of Canada’s plan to build a strong economy and greener future.
context: Department of Finance Canada, Carney government (Liberal), March 2025. The page is the government's own account; the reasons were political (affordability and "axe the tax" pressure) and are not stated in these quotes.

statement: For April 2025, the base Canada Carbon Rebate for a family of four was up to $456 (Alberta), with 412 in Saskatchewan, 330 in New Brunswick, 302 in Ontario, 300 in Manitoba, 298 in Newfoundland and Labrador and 220 in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, plus a 20 per cent rural top-up.
anchor: a family of four will receive up to $456 under the base Canada Carbon Rebate for April 2025
a rural top-up of 20 per cent is provided for individuals residing in small and rural communities.
locator: Table 1, April 2025 Canada Carbon Rebate Amounts (columns NL, PEI, NS, NB, ON, MB, SK, AB)
context: Department of Finance Canada, March 2025. Amounts are Canadian dollars per quarter, the final payment; Prince Edward Island's base already includes the rural supplement. Province-to-figure mapping follows the table's column order.

statement: On March 15, 2025, the Government of Canada stopped the federal fuel charge and the Canada Carbon Rebate for individuals, with no further quarterly payments after the April 2025 payment.
anchor: On March 15, 2025, the Government of Canada stopped the federal fuel charge and the Canada Carbon Rebate for individuals.
There will be no further quarterly CCR payments after the April 2025 payment.
context: Canada Revenue Agency page for the closed program, Carney government. The same page notes legislation tabled in November 2025 sets an October 30, 2026 filing cutoff for retroactive payments.

statement: The Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated that, counting only fiscal impacts, the average household in each province with the federal fuel charge would receive more from the Canada Carbon Rebate than it paid in 2030-31, a net gain ranging from 0.2 per cent of disposable income in Prince Edward Island to 1.0 per cent in Saskatchewan.
anchor: Considering only the fiscal impact of the federal fuel charge, PBO estimates that the average household in each of the backstop provinces
in 2030-31 will see a net gain, receiving more from the Canada Carbon Rebate than the total amount they pay in the federal fuel charge (directly and indirectly) and related Goods and Services Tax.
In 2030-31, the net gain for the average household in a backstop province ranges from 0.2 per cent of disposable income in Prince Edward Island to 1.0 per cent of disposable income in Saskatchewan.
locator: Key findings (first bullet); Section on fiscal impact
context: PBO, October 2024 (non-partisan; projection to 2030-31 at the planned C$170 rate). Averages by income quintile: PBO says each quintile gains except the top quintile in PEI, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and that individual households in a group do vary. This is an average, not a share of households; the Government's "most households come out ahead" figure is in a separate entry.

statement: When economic impacts were added, the Parliamentary Budget Officer estimated that in 2030-31 the average household in each province with the federal fuel charge would face a net cost ranging from 0.5 per cent of disposable income in New Brunswick to 0.7 per cent in Saskatchewan.
anchor: In 2030-31, taking into consideration both fiscal and economic impacts, PBO estimates that the average household in each of the backstop provinces will see a net cost, paying more in the federal fuel charge and related Goods and Services Tax, as well as receiving lower incomes (due to the fuel charge)
In 2030-31, the net cost for the average household in a backstop province ranges from 0.5 per cent of disposable income in New Brunswick to 0.7 per cent of disposable income in Saskatchewan.
context: PBO, October 2024. The "economic impact" (lost employment and investment income) is a general-equilibrium estimate from Environment and Climate Change Canada's EC-PRO model, not an observed cost. News headlines split on this report ("more in rebates than they pay" versus "worse off") because the two measures differ. The 2022-23 versions of the economic estimate had a modelling error, noted in a separate entry.

statement: The Parliamentary Budget Officer reported that its March 2022 and March 2023 household net-cost estimates including economic impacts reflected the broader economic impact of federal-equivalent carbon pricing, the fuel charge together with the industrial output-based pricing system, because both had been removed in the counterfactual scenario.
anchor: PBO staff discovered that both the fuel charge and OBPS had been removed in the counterfactual scenario. Consequently, estimates of household net costs incorporating “fiscal and economic impacts” published in our March 2022 and March 2023 reports, reflect the broader economic impact of federal-equivalent carbon pricing.
context: PBO's own correction note. It means the earlier "net loss for most households" headline (March 2023) mixed the fuel charge with industrial carbon pricing. The October 2024 update re-ran the economic part for the fuel charge alone and found lower net costs.

statement: The Parliamentary Budget Officer reported that Environment and Climate Change Canada estimated the fuel charge would account for almost 13 million tonnes of emissions reductions in 2030 and lower real GDP by 0.6 per cent compared with no fuel charge.
anchor: For the backstop provinces, Environment and Climate Change Canada estimates that the fuel charge will account for almost 13 million tonnes of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reductions in 2030 and will lower real gross domestic product (GDP) by 0.6 per cent relative to a scenario without the fuel charge, but with all other emissions-reduction measures maintained, including large-emitter trading systems.
context: A federal department's model estimate (Trudeau government), relayed by PBO; it is a projection, not a measurement of what the charge did. The real-GDP figure is a model result about the 2030 level.

statement: A 2024 Canadian Climate Institute report, as relayed by CBC, expected the consumer fuel charge to cut emissions by eight to 14 per cent, compared with 23 to 48 per cent for the industrial carbon price.
anchor: Yes, according to a 2024 report from the Canadian Climate Institute. It found that carbon pricing, both consumer and industrial, would play a “leading role” in cutting emissions by 2030.
The consumer carbon price, or fuel charge, was expected to cut emissions by eight to 14 per cent, compared to 23 to 48 per cent for the industrial carbon price.
locator: Section "Will emissions rise?" (second half of the article)
context: CBC News, 2025-04-02, summarizing an independent think tank's projection; the institute's report itself was not read. The ranges are projections to 2030. Industrial pricing continues; only the consumer charge ended.

statement: Using survey data from Canada and Switzerland, Mildenberger and co-authors found low public awareness and substantial underestimation of climate rebate amounts, and that perceptions of rebates were structured less by informed assessments of economic interest than by partisan identities.
anchor: show low public awareness and substantial underestimation of climate rebate amounts in both countries.
perceptions of climate rebates are structured less by informed assessments of economic interest than by partisan identities.
context: Peer-reviewed (Nature Climate Change, 2022), a five-wave Canadian panel plus a Swiss survey. In the Canadian experiment, telling respondents their true rebate did not raise support and led Conservative respondents to believe the policy imposed net costs on their household.

statement: In a March 20-22, 2024 survey of 1,602 Canadian adults, the Angus Reid Institute found that 44% of Canadians still felt they were not making as much back in rebates as they paid, while 19% said they saw a net benefit, up from 14% in November.
anchor: While awareness has risen, a plurality of Canadians still feel they are not making as much back as they pay (44%). There has, however, been a five-point increase in the number who say they see a net benefit from the program (14% to 19%).
The Angus Reid Institute conducted an online survey from March 20-22, 2024 among a representative randomized sample of 1,602 Canadian adults who are members of Angus Reid Forum.
locator: Text under "Plurality still believe tax paid outweighs rebate"; methodology note
context: Angus Reid Institute (self-commissioned, non-profit pollster), March 2024, an online panel. The article's table shows 19% got more back, 13% about break even, 44% paid more and 24% unsure in the full sample; so most did not say they came out ahead, but 44% rather than a majority said they lost.

statement: In a Nov. 10–14, 2023 survey of 2,512 adults, the Angus Reid Institute reported that the government said 80 per cent of eligible households receive more from the rebate than they pay in carbon taxes, while 54% of those who had received a rebate believed their household paid more in carbon taxes than it received.
anchor: The government says 80 per cent of eligible households receive more from the rebate than they pay in carbon taxes.
Of those who have received a household rebate, more than half (54%) believe their household paid more in carbon taxes than it received in rebates.
The Angus Reid Institute conducted an online survey from Nov. 10–14, 2023 among a representative randomized sample of 2,512 Canadian adults
locator: Text under rebate perceptions; methodology note
context: Angus Reid Institute, November 2023, self-commissioned. The 80% is the then-Trudeau government's claim as relayed by the pollster, not verified here; PBO's fiscal-only averages (separate entry) are consistent with a majority gaining but report quintile averages, not shares. Perception and measured outcome diverge.

statement: The European Commission reports that by the end of 2024 EU ETS emissions from electricity and heat generation and industrial manufacturing were 50% below 2005 levels, and that the system is on track to achieve its 2030 target of 62% reduction.
anchor: By the end of 2024, the EU ETS had helped drive down emissions from the electricity and heat generation and industrial manufacturing by 50% compared to 2005 levels.
With this progress, the system is on track to achieve the 2030 target of 62% reduction.
context: European Commission progress report (2025) on its own program. A measured emissions trend, not proof of what the carbon price alone caused: the same chapter credits renewables and nuclear for the 2024 power drop, and the 10% micro-study (Dechezleprêtre and others) is lower than the aggregate fall.

statement: EU ETS auction clearing prices averaged EUR 73.43 in 2025, up from EUR 64.74 in 2024, and in the first half of 2026 varied between EUR 62.19 and EUR 91.34.
anchor: The average price in 2025 was EUR 73.43, up from EUR 64.74 in 2024. In the first half of 2026, the price varied between EUR 62.19 and EUR 91.34.
locator: Section on auction prices (text under Figure 5)
context: European Commission report COM(2026) 596 on its auctions. ESMA's spot-price series gives EUR 74 for 2025 and EUR 65 for 2024 (secondary market).

statement: The average EU allowance price stood at EUR 64.8 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024, compared with EUR 83.6 in 2023.
anchor: The average price of EU allowances (EUAs) stood at EUR 64.8/t CO₂-eq in 2024, compared with EUR 83.6/t CO₂-eq in 2023.
locator: Section 2 (Allowance prices) of the Union Registry-based report
context: European Topic Centre for the European Environment Agency (2025), from Union Registry data. Together with the 2025 average of EUR 73.43 this gives the 2023-25 range; the price reached a two-year high near EUR 90 in January 2026 (ESMA).

statement: The annual average price of EU emission allowances was EUR 74 per tonne of CO2-equivalent emissions in 2025, up 13% from 2024.
anchor: The annual average price of EU emission allowances (EUAs) was EUR 74 per tonne of CO2-equivalent emissions in 2025, up 13% from 2024.
context: ESMA, the EU securities regulator, annual carbon-market report (2026), based on market data. Independent of the Commission's auction figures but consistent with them.

statement: Revenues from the EU ETS rose to EUR 43.2 billion in 2025, 11% above 2024, and for the first time EUR 3.7 billion was raised for the Social Climate Fund.
anchor: Revenues from the EU ETS increased further in 2025, rising up to EUR 43.2 billion (+11% compared to 2024), confirming the system’s key role as a powerful financing engine.
For the first time in 2025, EUR 3.7 billion were raised also for the Social Climate Fund, to support vulnerable households and transport users during the transition to climate neutrality.
context: European Commission report COM(2026) 596. More than half went to Member State budgets; the rest to the Innovation and Modernisation Funds, the Recovery and Resilience Facility and the new Social Climate Fund.

statement: Member States must use all ETS revenue, or an equivalent financial value, for climate and energy action; of the €24.4 billion that went directly to Member States in 2024, €3.2 billion (13%) financed aid to electricity-intensive industries for indirect carbon costs.
anchor: Member States are required to use all collected ETS revenues, or an equivalent financial value, to support climate and energy action.
In 2024, the total auction revenue amounted to €38.8 billion, with €24.4 billion going directly to Member States.
This is because €3.2 billion of the 2024 revenue (13%) was reported to have financed aid for electricity-intensive industries for indirect carbon costs
context: European Commission page (2026). EU ETS revenue goes to climate and energy spending and state budgets, not to per-person dividends; this is the contrast with the Swiss and Canadian designs.

statement: The Commission reports that the surrendering obligation under ETS2, the new system for buildings and road transport fuels, was postponed by one year from 2027 to 2028, with the first surrendering by 31 May 2029.
anchor: With the amendment to the European Climate Law adopted in spring 2026 10, the surrendering obligation under ETS2 was postponed by one year from 2027 to 2028.
The first surrendering will take place by 31 May 2029.
context: European Commission report COM(2026) 596. The same report says ETS2 auctions can start early (2027) to make revenue available, and that the Commission is updating its assessment of ETS2's impacts after the European Council's October conclusions. The quote's "10" is a footnote marker in the source.

statement: The Social Climate Fund, with a mandatory minimum 25% contribution by Member States to their plans, will make at least EUR 86.7 billion available over the 2026-2032 period.
anchor: Combined with a mandatory minimum 25% contribution by Member States to their plans, the SCF will make at least EUR 86.7 billion available over the 2026-2032 period.
context: European Commission report COM(2026) 596. The Fund's own contribution is smaller (the Commission's 2025 report gives EUR 65 billion before the national share).

statement: In the Social Climate Plans endorsed or submitted so far, more than 90% of the fund goes to long-lasting investments in buildings and road transport and less than 10% to direct income support, well below the legal limit of 37.5%.
anchor: more than 90% of the fund is used for supporting long lasting investments in the decarbonisation of the buildings and road transport sectors
less than 10% of the fund being devoted to Direct Income Support (DIS), well below the legal limit of 37.5%.
context: European Commission report COM(2026) 596, analysing 5 endorsed and 6 submitted plans (roughly EUR 20 billion of funding); the remaining Member States had not finished. Direct per-person payments are a small share by choice of Member States.

statement: The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its definitive phase on 1 January 2026, and sales of CBAM certificates will start on 1 February 2027.
anchor: CBAM entered its definitive phase as of 1 January 2026.
Sales of CBAM certificates will start on 1 February 2027.
locator: Section on definitive regime and Section 3.1
context: European Commission Q&A for importers. During the transitional period (October 2023 to December 2025) importers only reported embedded emissions, with no financial obligation. A Commission legislative proposal to revise CBAM was adopted in December 2025.

statement: Dechezleprêtre, Nachtigall and Venmans found the EU ETS was associated with a statistically significant reduction in regulated installations' carbon emissions of about 10% between 2005 and 2012 (sensitivity range 7% to 16%) and no statistically significant impact on regulated firms' employees and profit.
anchor: Our results suggest that the introduction of the EU ETS was associated with a statistically significant reduction of carbon emissions in the order of −10% in the first two trading phases between 2005 and 2012, with sensitivity tests pointing to effects between −7% and −16%.
did not have a statistically significant impact on regulated firms' number of employees and profit
context: Peer-reviewed (Journal of Environmental Economics and Management, 2023); OECD and LSE authors. Covers the low-price, free-allocation early phases (average about EUR 20) and a small sample; the authors say it is unknown whether it holds at 2025 prices near EUR 74. The Commission's 50% aggregate fall is a different measure.

statement: The same Dechezleprêtre team notes its emissions result rests on 240 ETS installations and 280 non-ETS installations in four countries and is significant only at the 10% level in its preferred specification.
anchor: our results are based on a relatively small sample of 240 ETS installations and 280 non ETS installations.
the results in our preferred specification, though robust across a number of alternative specifications, are only significant at the 10% level because of the small sample size.
context: Authors' own caveat in the 2023 paper; the four countries are France, the Netherlands, Norway and the United Kingdom. Same research team as the previous entry, so not independent corroboration of it.

statement: Using 30 years of data on carbon taxation in various European countries, Metcalf and Stock found no evidence of a negative impact on employment or GDP growth, but rather a zero to modest positive impact.
anchor: We estimate the macroeconomic impacts of carbon taxes on GDP and employment growth rates using 30 years of data on carbon taxation in various European countries.
We find no evidence for a negative impact on employment or GDP growth but rather find a zero to modest positive impact.
context: Peer-reviewed (American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics, vol. 15(3), 2023); Tufts and Harvard economists. European carbon taxes were modest in rate and covered about 30% of emissions. Metcalf also wrote the BC paper, so the two are not independent of each other.

statement: Metcalf and Stock found a cumulative emissions reduction on the order of 4 to 6 percent for a $40/ton carbon dioxide tax covering 30 percent of emissions.
anchor: a cumulative emissions reduction on the order of 4 to 6 percent for a $40/ton
tax covering 30 percent of emissions.
context: Peer-reviewed (2023). The authors say a broad-based U.S. tax would likely do more, since European taxes typically do not cover the sectors with the lowest abatement costs. The brief called this AEJ: Policy; the journal is AEJ: Macroeconomics.

statement: Switzerland's carbon dioxide levy has been CHF 120 per tonne since 2022, raising around CHF 1.2 billion a year, of which 55% is redistributed to the public and the private sector and 45% funds buildings, renewable energy and innovative companies.
anchor: The levy has been set at CHF 120 per tonne
since 2022. This results in annual revenue of around CHF 1.2 billion.
45% of the revenue is used to reduce carbon emissions in buildings (Buildings Programme), fund renewable energy and promote innovative companies (Technology Fund).
55% of the revenue is redistributed to the public and the private sector based on the levy burden, which is determined statistically.
locator: Page text (CO2 levy for private individuals)
context: Swiss Federal Office for the Environment (2026). The levy applies to heating and process fuels, not petrol or diesel (the same office's separate page says importers instead partly offset transport emissions). Earlier descriptions put the redistributed share at two-thirds.

statement: Switzerland refunds the carbon dioxide levy paid by the public equally to all residents insured under the Federal Health Insurance Act, as an offset against their health insurance premium, so every person receives the same amount regardless of energy use.
anchor: is redistributed equally to all persons resident in Switzerland who are insured under the Federal Health Insurance Act (HIA).
Insured persons get notification of the amount they are to receive when they are informed of their health insurance premium. The amount is offset against the premium.
context: Swiss Federal Office for the Environment (2026). This is the one national equal per-person climate refund in operation besides Canada's (now closed). Mildenberger and co-authors found Swiss residents also underestimate it, because it arrives as a premium credit rather than a payment.

statement: For 2027 the Swiss government will pass on CHF 527 million to the public, which equates to CHF 57 per person, from the carbon dioxide and solvent (VOC) levies.
anchor: In 2027, a total of CHF 527 million will be passed on to the public. This equates to CHF 57 per person.
context: Swiss Federal Office for the Environment. A planned amount for 2027 covering both levies; the per-person refund is small compared with the levy's size.

statement: France's carbon tax of 44,60 euros per tonne of CO2 was due to rise to 55 euros on 1 January 2019, and the Élysée announced that the 2019 increase was cancelled.
anchor: La taxe carbone, un prélèvement pesant sur les produits énergétiques selon leur niveau d'émission de CO2, devait passer de 44,60 à 55 euros la tonne de CO2 au 1er janvier 2019.
L'Elysée a annoncé, mercredi soir, l'annulation de l'augmentation de la taxe carbone pour 2019.
context: French public-service news report of 2018-12-06 on the response to the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) protests against fuel-tax rises under President Macron.

statement: On 18 December the French National Assembly validated freezing fuel taxes until 2022, removing the planned 2019 rise of 3 centimes per litre on petrol and 6 on diesel, and by 2022 a total of 10 centimes on petrol and 19 on diesel.
anchor: L'Assemblée nationale a validé ce mardi 18 décembre le gel des taxes sur les carburants jusqu'en 2022.
Cela revient à supprimer la hausse en 2019 de 3 centimes sur l'essence et 6 centimes sur le gazole, et au total, d'ici à 2022, de 10 centimes sur l'essence et de 19 centimes sur le gazole.
context: Ouest-France with AFP, 2018-12-18, French-language. A later finance law could restore the rise after 2019; the report notes this possibility. The freeze came after the Senate had voted it and followed the yellow-vest protests.

statement: Australia's Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2014, part of a package of 8 bills to remove the carbon pricing mechanism, repealed the six Acts that established it and finally passed both Houses on 17 Jul 2014.
anchor: Part of a package of 8 bills to remove the carbon pricing mechanism, the bill: repeals the six Acts which established the carbon pricing mechanism
Finally passed both Houses | 17 Jul 2014
context: Official Parliament of Australia bill page; Abbott government (Liberal-National) bill repealing the Gillard-era carbon price. The page does not give the price level; secondary sources give about A$23 per tonne at the start in 2012.

statement: RenewEconomy reported that the Australian Energy Regulator said the electricity market cut emissions by 10.3 per cent in the two years of the carbon price, but that these gains have been eroded since the carbon price was dumped, while noting structural shifts such as falling demand.
anchor: saying that the Australian electricity market cut emissions by 10.3 per cent in the two years of the carbon price, but these gains have been eroded since the carbon price was dumped.
the electricity market is experiencing structural shifts
context: Trade-press report of a regulator's annual market report (2014); the regulator's own report was not read. Covers the electricity sector only, not the whole economy, and mixes the price effect with falling demand and rooftop solar.

statement: Vox reported that carbon dioxide emissions from Australia's power sector dropped roughly 9 percent in the first six months after the carbon tax took effect, but called the drop unsustainable.
anchor: Carbon-dioxide emissions from the power sector dropped roughly 9 percent in the first six months after the tax went into effect.
But in a lot of ways, that drop was unsustainable.
locator: Section "The rise and fall of Australia's carbon tax"
context: Explanatory news piece (2014) relaying University of Melbourne analysis: hydropower was over-dispatched under the tax and brown coal returned after repeal. It qualifies the size of the sustained effect.

statement: Washington voters rejected Initiative 732, a revenue-neutral carbon tax, on November 8, 2016 with 59.25% voting against, and Initiative 1631, a carbon fee with earmarked revenue, on November 8, 2018 with 56.56% against.
anchor: I-732 was rejected on November 8, 2016, with 59.25% of the votes against.
I-1631 was rejected with 56.56% of the votes against on November 8, 2018.
context: NBER working paper (2025), reporting official vote shares; the paper is not peer reviewed. I-732 replicated BC's revenue-neutral design and was opposed by some environmental groups; I-1631 earmarked revenue for environmental purposes and was opposed by oil companies. The paper finds support rose 10 to 20 points by 2024 in every block group.

statement: Washington voters rejected Initiative Measure No. 2117 on November 5, 2024, which would have repealed the cap-and-invest program, with 2,340,077 votes (61.95%) against and 1,437,103 (38.05%) in favor.
anchor: November 5, 2024 General Election Results
Initiative Measure No. 2117 County Results & Map
locator: Initiative Measure No. 2117 block (Measures - All Results)
context: Washington Secretary of State, certified results (existing catalog row SRC-3393). The initiative would have repealed the 2021 Climate Commitment Act and barred state cap-and-trade; its description comes from the ballot title, not from this table. NBER (2025) reports proponents outspent opponents about $23 million to $15 million.

statement: California Assembly Bill 1207, approved September 19, 2025, extends the state's market-based compliance mechanism until January 1, 2046 and states the Legislature's intent that it be known as the California Cap-and-Invest Program.
anchor: Assembly Bill No. 1207
[ Approved by Governor September 19, 2025. Filed with Secretary of State September 19, 2025. ]
This bill would extend the above-described provisions until January 1, 2046.
The bill would state the intent of the Legislature that the market-based compliance mechanism be known as the California Cap-and-Invest Program.
context: California primary law (Chapter 117, Statutes of 2025), signed by Governor Newsom. The bill also directs revenue from price-ceiling sales to a fund for direct rebates and household energy-cost investments. The brief's "extended to 2045" matches the governor's release; the statute runs to January 1, 2046.

statement: RGGI, Inc. reports that carbon dioxide emissions from the power sector in the ten fully participating RGGI states have fallen by 43% compared to a 2006-2008 baseline, faster than the emissions reduction across the U.S. as a whole.
anchor: emissions from these states have fallen by 43% compared to a 2006-2008 baseline, faster than the emissions reduction across the U.S. as a whole.
locator: Page text under chart "CO2 Emissions in the RGGI 10 States"
context: The program administrator's own account (a nonprofit run for the member states). Other RGGI figures quoted in news differ by baseline and states: 46% since 2009 (Bloomberg Law, 2025) and about 53% through 2024 (RGGI's executive director). The fall is not all caused by the price (next entry).

statement: RGGI's executive director said that across all states that participated from 2009 there is about a 53% emissions reduction through 2024, while a Clean Energy New Hampshire director noted RGGI launched at the same time as the fracking revolution.
anchor: If we're looking at all the states that participated in RGGI, from 2009 to the present, we're looking at about a 53% [carbon emissions] reduction through 2024,
It's important to remember that RGGI launched right at the same time as the fracking revolution came about
locator: Section "Sixteen years in, it's worked pretty well"
context: Public-radio report (Marketplace, 2025) with two stakeholders: the program's head and a clean-energy advocate who cautions that cheap natural gas also cut coal burning. Different headline numbers from the previous entry arise from different baselines.

statement: Bloomberg Law reported that a Pennsylvania budget bill signed by Gov. Josh Shapiro on Nov. 12 took the state out of RGGI, and that member states have raised more than $6 billion from auctions.
anchor: The national political outlook and the price-hike narrative helped drive a budget bill in Pennsylvania that took the state out of RGGI, which Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) signed Nov. 12.
member states have raised more than $6 billion from auctions, which has been poured back into communities for everything from bill assistance to clean transportation projects, the program says.
context: Bloomberg Law, December 2, 2025. Pennsylvania's exit followed rising electricity prices that, per the article, have stalled RGGI's growth; Virginia's governor-elect was expected to rejoin. The $6 billion is RGGI's own figure ("the program says").

statement: Treasury's Office of Tax Analysis modelled a sample carbon tax starting at $49 per metric ton in 2019 and rising to $70 in 2028, estimating net revenues of $194 billion in the first year and $583 per person if the revenue were rebated to individuals.
anchor: a carbon tax that started at $49 per metric ton of carbon dioxide equivalent (mt CO2-e) in 2019 and
increased to $70 in 2028. We estimate that such a tax would generate net revenues of $194 billion in the
portion of the payroll tax. If the revenue were rebated to individuals it would amount to $583 per person
context: Treasury Office of Tax Analysis Working Paper 115 (January 2017), career staff in the closing weeks of the Obama administration; a methodology paper, not Treasury policy. Dollars are U.S. dollars per metric ton CO2-e. This is where the $583 per person ($2,300 for a family of four) scale comes from.

statement: Treasury's distribution model estimated that combining a carbon tax with a per person rebate would raise the poorest decile's after-tax income by almost 9 percent and lower the top decile's by 1 percent.
anchor: change in tax burdens. The TDM estimates that the poorest decile would experience almost a 9 percent
increase in average after-tax income compared to a 1 percent decrease in average after-tax income for
the top income decile.
context: Treasury OTA working paper (January 2017). Estimates for an illustrative swap, "chosen solely for illustrative purposes". The paper gives decile averages; the commonly repeated "about 70% of households come out ahead" does not appear as a sentence in this text and is attributed to Treasury second-hand by RFF and the Climate Leadership Council.

statement: Treasury's distribution model estimated that the carbon tax alone cuts after-tax income by 0.8 percent in the lowest income decile and by 1.8 percent in the 9th decile, a burden rising with income through the 9th decile, and judged this less regressive than the Tax Policy Center (2013) and CBO (2012) distributions.

context: Treasury OTA working paper (January 2017). This model passes the tax back to workers and capital owners, not to consumer prices; the paper itself says CBO and the Tax Policy Center find a more regressive pattern under price pass-through. Present both views.

statement: Resources for the Future's explainer states that a study by the US Treasury predicted that approximately 70 percent of households would be better off with an equal per capita dividend.
anchor: A study by the US Treasury predicted that approximately 70 percent of households would be better off with an equal per capita dividend.
Carbon dividends are an especially progressive, or equitable, use of the revenue
context: Resources for the Future (nonpartisan research nonprofit), explainer dated September 2019, repeating a Treasury result second-hand. The brief listed an RFF 2021 analysis; none was found. Treat the 70% as an attributed figure until the Treasury table is located.

statement: The Climate Leadership Council's plan proposes an economy-wide carbon fee starting at $40 a ton (2017$) and rising 5% a year above inflation, with all net proceeds returned equally and quarterly, about $2,000 for a family of four in the first year.
anchor: starting at $40 a ton (2017$) and increasing every year at 5% above inflation.
All net proceeds from the carbon fee will be returned to the American people on an equal and quarterly basis.
A family of four will receive approximately $2,000 in carbon dividend payments in the first year.
context: Advocacy group's own proposal (updated September 2019); the plan is a position, and the $2,000 is the group's own estimate. Its scale is consistent with Treasury's $583 per person.

statement: The Climate Leadership Council states that over two-thirds of American households would be financial winners under a carbon dividends plan, citing a US Treasury finding that 70% of American households would benefit.
anchor: over two-thirds of American households would be financial winners under a carbon dividends plan
the US Treasury found that 70% of American households would benefit, because on average they would receive more in dividend payments than they would pay in increased energy prices.
context: Advocacy paper (2024) from a group that backs the policy; its other page says "8 in 10 households come out ahead" using Oxford Economics. Share-of-winners figures depend on household size, which equal per-person dividends reward for larger families.

statement: Goulder and co-authors found that, once source-side and use-side effects are combined, the progressive source-side impacts tend to offset fully the regressive use-side impacts of a carbon tax, and that distributional impacts depend importantly on how the revenue is recycled.
anchor: the use-side impacts tend to be regressive while the source-side impacts are progressive, and the progressive source-side impacts tend to offset fully the regressive use-side impacts.
Our results indicate that the distributional impacts depend importantly on the nature of revenue-recycling and the treatment of transfer income.
context: Peer-reviewed general-equilibrium study (Journal of Public Economics, 2019; Stanford, RFF and UCLA authors); the brief said PNAS. A model result, not an observed outcome. Treasury's pass-back assumption points the same direction.

statement: CBO said the effects of a carbon tax on the U.S. economy would depend on how the revenues were used, and estimated that a $20 per metric ton price in 2012 rising 5.6 percent a year would yield a total of $1.2 trillion over 2012–2021.
anchor: The effects of a carbon tax on the U.S. economy would depend on how the revenues from the tax were used.

CBO estimated in 2011 that setting a price of $20 per metric ton on greenhouse gas emissions in the United States in 2012 and raising that price at a nominal rate of 5.6 percent per year would yield a total of $1.2 trillion in revenues over the 2012–2021 period.
context: Congressional Budget Office (nonpartisan), May 2013. The revenue estimate dates from CBO's 2011 options report. The report adds that using revenue to relieve selected groups would not lower the total economic cost, a trade-off against tax-rate cuts.

statement: CBO estimated that a $20 emission charge would reduce total U.S. CO2 emissions between 2012 and 2021 by about 8 percent.
anchor: That $20 emission charge would reduce total U.S. emissions of CO2 between 2012 and 2021 by about 8 percent, CBO estimated.
context: Congressional Budget Office (nonpartisan), May 2013, a projection from its 2011 analysis. A cap-and-trade-style price in $2012; the response in real life may differ.

statement: Princeton's REPEAT Project (2022) found the U.S. high-voltage transmission system needs to grow 2.3% a year, up from 1% a year over the last decade, to meet the IRA's emissions reduction potential, and that the potential falls by 80% if transmission additions stay unchanged and by 25% if growth rises only to 1.5% a year.
anchor: The U.S. high-voltage transmission system needs to grow 2.3% a year, up from its 1% annual growth rate over the last decade, to meet the Inflation Reduction Act’s greenhouse gas emissions reduction potential
falls by 80% if the pace of transmission additions remains unchanged and falls by 25% if transmission growth increases to only 1.5% a year
locator: Utility Dive, first and second bullets
context: Modeling analysis by the Princeton-led REPEAT Project (Jenkins and others, September 2022), reported by Utility Dive. A university-led model of the 2022 IRA, not peer reviewed; the results depend on the model's assumptions about generation costs and siting, and the IRA was changed by P.L. 119-21 in 2025. The 1% historical rate is the project's own figure.

statement: DOE's 2023 National Transmission Needs Study found median model results show interregional transfer capacity must grow by 25% to meet moderate load and clean energy growth, by 114% for moderate load and high clean energy growth, and by 412% for high load growth by 2035.
anchor:
Median capacity expansion results
show interregional transfer capacity must grow by 25% to meet future moderate load and clean
energy growth, by 114% to meet moderate load and high clean energy growth, and by 412% to
meet high load growth futures by 2035.
context: Biden administration DOE Grid Deployment Office, October 2023. Synthesizes six capacity-expansion models; the three scenario groups are assumptions about load and clean energy growth, not forecasts, and DOE says the high-load group will not be realized "without additional state and federal policies". The study predates P.L. 119-21 and the 2025 reversals.

statement: DOE's 2023 National Transmission Needs Study found that in futures enabled by the IIJA and IRA, median model results suggest 54,500 GW-mi of new within-region transmission will be needed nationwide by 2035, a 64% increase from today's transmission system.
anchor:
median
model results suggest 54,500 GW-mi of new within-region transmission will be needed

context: Biden administration DOE, October 2023; model median for the moderate-load, high-clean-energy scenario group, which assumes the IIJA and IRA as enacted in 2021-22. The 2025 law cut IRA credits, so the "high clean energy growth" assumption is weaker for 2029 than DOE assumed.

statement: NERC's 2024 Interregional Transfer Capability Study recommended 35 GW of additional transfer capability across the United States to strengthen energy adequacy under extreme conditions.
anchor: An additional 35 GW of transfer capability is recommended across the United States as a vehicle to strengthen energy adequacy under extreme conditions
locator: ITCS final report, Executive Summary, key findings
context: NERC, the industry-funded, FERC-certified reliability organization, November 2024 (Biden-era; directed by Congress in the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act). It is a reliability study under stated assumptions, "not a transmission plan or blueprint", and excludes economic, permitting and policy considerations; NERC also says transmission upgrades alone will not address all risks and that local resources, storage and demand-side options belong in the mix.

statement: NERC's 2024 study identified potential energy deficiency in all 12 weather years it evaluated and in 11 different transmission planning regions, with a maximum resource deficiency of almost 19 gigawatts in ERCOT.
anchor: Potential for energy deficiency 25 was identified in all 12 weather years evaluated and in 11 different TPRs, with a maximum resource deficiency of almost 19 gigawatts (GW) in ERCOT.
locator: ITCS final report, Executive Summary, Figure ES.4 text
context: NERC, November 2024, under common modeled assumptions about future load and generation; the "25" in the quotation is a footnote marker in the report. Deficiency means modeled energy shortfall in extreme weather, not forecast outages.

statement: FERC issued Order No. 1920 on May 13, 2024 to improve regional electric transmission planning and cost allocation, issued rehearing Order No. 1920-A on November 21, 2024, and issued a second rehearing order, Order No. 1920-B, on April 11, 2025.
anchor: On May 13, 2024, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) issued a final rule, Order No. 1920, [1] to improve regional electric transmission planning and cost allocation.
the Commission addressed in a rehearing order, Order No. 1920-A, [2] on November 21, 2024.
on April 11, 2025, the Commission issued a second rehearing order, Order No. 1920-B.
context: FERC (independent commission; the Order was issued under the Biden administration, the second rehearing under the second Trump administration). Primary dates.

statement: As of November 2026, challenges to Order Nos. 1920, 1920-A and 1920-B are consolidated in Appalachian Voices v. FERC, No. 24-1650(L) in the Fourth Circuit; oral argument occurred on September 15, 2026 and the court has not yet issued a merits decision.
anchor: Petitions for review of Order Nos. 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B are consolidated in Appalachian Voices v. FERC, No. 24-1650(L) (4th Cir.). Oral argument occurred on September 15, 2026. The court has not yet issued a merits decision.
context: Harvard Law School's Environmental and Energy Law Program tracker (nonpartisan, secondary). Petitioners run in both directions (some seek vacatur, others say the rule does not go far enough). The tracker adds that FERC has granted region-specific compliance extensions; the first planning cycles will not start until after 2027.

statement: The CATF and Niskanen Center study of transmission permitting compiled case studies of 37 transmission projects under NEPA review from 2010 to 2020 and concluded NEPA is not a primary driver of delay; government-wide only 0.22% of NEPA decisions get litigated.
anchor: The research team compiled case studies of 37 transmission projects under NEPA review from 2010 to 2020
Government-wide, only 0.22% of NEPA decisions get litigated
our independent research efforts show NEPA is not a primary driver of delay
locator: Niskanen article, summary paragraphs and findings
context: Niskanen Center (think tank) with Clean Air Task Force (clean-energy advocacy nonprofit), August 2024. Both have a stake in the conclusion; the sample is 37 federally reviewed transmission lines, and the authors say litigation can be impactful when it happens (plaintiffs win about a quarter of suits). Delays are attributed to staffing, funding and coordination gaps.

statement: LBNL's latest Queued Up report (data through the end of 2024) found that only 13% of capacity that requested interconnection from 2000 to 2019 had reached commercial operations by the end of 2024, 77% had been withdrawn and 10% was still active.
anchor: Only 13% of capacity that submitted interconnection requests from 2000-2019 had reached commercial operations by the end of 2024; 77% of that capacity had been withdrawn and 10% was still active.
context: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (DOE lab), December 2025 edition with data through end of 2024; the lab says it makes no policy recommendations. High withdrawal partly reflects speculative and duplicate requests, so the completion rate is not the same as unmet demand.

statement: LBNL found the typical project built in 2024 took 55 months from interconnection request to commercial operations, compared to 36 months in 2015 and 22 months in 2008.
anchor: The typical project built in 2024 took 55 months from the interconnection request to commercial operations1, compared to 36 months in 2015 and 22 months in 2008
context: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (DOE lab), December 2025; "1" is a footnote marker in the report. Projects built in a given year are survivors; the lab notes timelines are longer in most but not all regions, with ERCOT and non-ISO areas faster.

statement: CEQ (2020) reviewed 1,276 environmental impact statements finalized between 2010 and 2018 and found the average time from notice of intent to record of decision was 4.5 years, with half taking longer than 3.5 years.

CEQ reviewed 1,276 EISs for which a notice of availability of a final EIS was published
between January 1, 2010 and December 31, 2018

CEQ found that across all Federal agencies, the average EIS completion time (from NOI
to ROD) was 4.5 years.
Half took longer than 3.5 years to complete;
locator: CEQ fact sheet, Background and Findings
context: Council on Environmental Quality, first Trump administration, June 2020. Covers all agencies and project types, so it says little about wind and solar, and only the EISs finished by June 2019; it measures elapsed time, not the share caused by agency staffing or applicant delay. The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 later set two-year limits for EISs.

statement: Resources for the Future found solar and wind projects required 27 and 45 months to complete the NEPA EIS process, against a CEQ average of 54 months, and that NEPA-reviewed solar projects account for roughly 10 percent of solar capacity added and wind projects 3.7 percent.
anchor: Compared with the CEQ average of 54 months for all project types, solar and wind projects required 27 and 45 months, respectively, to complete the NEPA EIS process

NEPA-reviewed solar projects account for only roughly 10 percent of the total increase in solar capacity, and NEPA-reviewed wind projects account for only 3.7 percent of the total increase in wind capacity over the study period
context: Resources for the Future (nonpartisan economics think tank), 2024; review of solar, wind and geothermal projects under the 1978 NEPA rules through 2023. The study notes a third of solar and half of wind EIS projects exceeded two years, the longest took 12 years, and early-stage review information is limited. Only a small share of projects face federal NEPA review at all.

statement: The Sabin Center at Columbia Law School found, through the end of 2025, at least 888 state and local restrictions blocking renewable energy projects and at least 567 projects facing significant local opposition across 48 states.
anchor: finds that at least 888 state and local restrictions blocking renewable energy projects had been adopted and that there were at least 567 projects that faced significant local opposition, across 48 states, by the end of 2025
context: Columbia Law School's Sabin Center, 6th edition (September 2, 2026). A tally of cases the authors found, "at least", not a census; the Center runs a program that defends renewable projects against such opposition. Earlier editions counted 395 local restrictions (2023 data) and 459 (2024 data), partly reflecting wider searching.

statement: The Sabin Center reported that between 2018 and 2023 at least 30% of utility-scale wind and solar projects were cancelled during the siting process, largely because of community opposition, local ordinances and zoning.
anchor: Between 2018-2023, at least 30% of utility-scale wind and solar projects were cancelled during the siting process, largely because of community opposition, local ordinances, and zoning.
context: Sabin Center (Columbia Law School), July 2025 press page for the fifth edition; the 30% figure is cited from other research whose method this page does not give. A pro-siting program's account; the page does not name the underlying study.

statement: As reported by the Sabin Center, a January 2024 LBNL survey of utility-scale wind and solar developers identified local ordinances, grid interconnection and community opposition as the three leading causes of project cancellation.
anchor: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s January 2024 Survey of Utility-Scale Wind and Solar Developers Report, which identified local ordinances, grid interconnection, and community opposition as the three leading causes of cancelation of wind and solar projects.
locator: Sabin June 2024 report, section on prior research
context: Quoted second-hand from Columbia's Sabin Center (June 2024 edition); the LBNL survey itself (DOE lab, developer self-reports, about 120 respondents per WRI) was not read. Developer opinion, not project outcomes.

statement: The TVA Act authorizes TVA to issue bonds in an amount not exceeding $30,000,000,000 outstanding at any one time; a 1979 law raised the limit from $15,000,000,000.
anchor: The Corporation is authorized to issue and sell bonds, notes, and other evidences of indebtedness (hereinafter collectively referred to as “bonds”) in an amount not exceeding $30,000,000,000 outstanding at any one time to assist in financing its power program and to refund such bonds.
context: Primary law as codified (U.S. Code, 2026 edition). Bonds are not guaranteed by the federal government. TVA can also finance through leases that do not count against the limit (see EV-CLP-417).

statement: TVA's FY2025 annual report states that bonds outstanding were $22.1 billion at September 30, 2025, against a statutory limit of $30.0 billion.
anchor: in an amount not to exceed $30.0 billion outstanding at any time.

context: TVA's own SEC filing for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2025 (filed November 2025). TVA notes that other financing, such as certain lease financings, is not subject to the limit and could supplement bonds. The FY2026 report is due around the recheck date.

statement: TVA operates the nation's largest public power system: at September 30, 2025 it had 62 directly served customers and 153 local power company customers serving approximately 10 million people in parts of seven southeastern states, and 2025 electricity sales revenue of $13.5 billion.

in 2025 revenues from the sale of electricity totaled $13.5 billion.
context: TVA's own SEC filing (federal corporation, FY ended September 30, 2025).

statement: TVA's own FY2025 annual report says residential rates are lower than those paid by over 80% of customers of the top 100 U.S. utilities and industrial rates are lower than those paid by 90% of customers of the top 100 utilities.
anchor: Residential rates are lower than those paid by over 80% of customers of the top 100 U.S. utilities. Industrial rates are lower than those paid by 90% of customers of the top 100 utilities.
context: TVA's own comparison, built from EIA data, by an agency with a stake in the result; a ranking of rates, not of costs, and TVA's low rates sit alongside its cap on bonds and its history of cost overruns. Its February 2026 investor deck puts TVA's residential rate at 12.71 cents per kilowatt-hour, 21st of the top 100 (April 2025 rolling average), but that deck was not recorded as a source.

statement: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act gave BPA a permanent $10 billion increase in its Treasury borrowing authority, with $6 billion available immediately and $4 billion at the start of FY 2028, bringing the total to $17.7 billion in 2028.

locator: BPA Debt Management page, "Federal debt management"
context: Bonneville Power Administration, a federal power marketing administration within DOE; describes a 2021 law. Borrowing is repaid from power and transmission rates, not appropriations.

statement: WAPA's Transmission Infrastructure Program manages WAPA's statutory $3.25 billion borrowing authority and can make strategic loans for qualifying transmission projects.
anchor: TIP manages WAPA’s statutory $3.25 billion borrowing authority and can make strategic loans to project applicants for qualifying projects
context: Western Area Power Administration, a federal power marketing administration within DOE. Granted by Congress in 2009 (WAPA testimony, May 2023, not recorded as a source).

statement: In 2023 public power utilities served 15.3% of U.S. electric customers, cooperatives 13.4% and investor-owned utilities 65.7%.
locator: 2025 Public Power Statistical Report, "Number of Customers by Utility Type, 2023"
context: American Public Power Association (trade association for public power), 2025 report, tabulating EIA Forms 861 and 861S for 2023. statement: By January 2025 USDA said it had awarded roughly 90% of New ERA funding, obligating approximately $9 billion of the program's $9.7 billion budget authority to rural electric cooperatives.
anchor: USDA has now awarded roughly 90% of total available New ERA funding to benefit rural electric cooperatives and their members, obligating approximately $9 billion of the program’s $9.7 billion budget authority.
locator: USDA press release, "New ERA Investments" section
context: Biden administration USDA release, January 10, 2025, about a program created by the 2022 IRA. Obligation of awards, not money paid or projects built; the release's project, jobs and emissions figures are USDA projections and were not used.

statement: In late March 2025 USDA asked New ERA grant winners to submit revised plans within 30 days eliminating Biden-era DEIA and climate mandates embedded in previous proposals; High Country News reported the revisions were voluntary.

statement: New York's 2023-24 enacted state budget gave the New York Power Authority new authority to develop, own and operate renewable energy generating projects, supporting the state goal of producing 70% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030.
anchor: The 2023-24 Enacted State Budget provides the New York Power Authority (NYPA) with new authority to develop, own, and operate renewable energy generating projects—either alone or in collaboration with other entities—to assist the state in meeting its bold clean energy targets, including producing 70% of the state’s electricity from renewable sources by 2030
context: New York Power Authority, May 3, 2023, describing the state budget law (the Build Public Renewables Act provisions); a state government source. The quotation is longer than the usual limit because it is a single sentence, and trimming it would lose the figures.

statement: In December 2025 NYPA's board approved an updated renewables strategic plan with opportunities totaling nearly 5.5 GW of combined capacity, a pipeline NYPA says it will advance only where projects are technically and financially viable.

ultimately only advance those that are deemed technically and financially viable
locator: NYPA press release, headline and second paragraph

statement: DOE issued a $465 million loan to Tesla Motors in January 2010; DOE's investor deck says the taxpayer-funded loan was repaid early and in full.

Taxpayer-funded loan was repaid early, and in full

statement: Solyndra received a $535 million DOE loan guarantee and filed for bankruptcy in September 2011.

experienced severe construction delays and cost overruns.

Unit 3 entered service more than seven years behind schedule

statement: DOE says the Loan Programs Office operates as the Office of Energy Dominance Financing and that the new office possesses all of the authorities and receives all of the appropriations assigned to the Loan Programs Office.

statement: DOE's interim final rule of October 2025 says the Energy Dominance Financing provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act authorize the Secretary to guarantee loans of up to a total principal amount of $250 billion through September 30, 2028.
anchor: The Energy Dominance Financing provisions of OBBBA amended section 1706 to now authorize the Secretary of Energy (“Secretary”) to guarantee loans of up to a total principal amount of $250 billion through September 30, 2028.
locator: Interim final rule, Background, "One Big Beautiful Bill Act"

statement: On July 23, 2025 DOE announced that its Loan Programs Office had terminated its conditional commitment for the Grain Belt Express Phase 1 transmission line, which would have provided a loan guarantee of up to $4.9 billion.
anchor: has terminated its conditional commitment for the Grain Belt Express Phase 1 project
a taxpayer-funded loan guarantee of up to $4.9 billion

Reuters reported farmers' opposition to the guarantee over eminent-domain filings. The termination is a fact; the reasons are contested.

statement: DOE's Transmission Facilitation Program page says DOE announced $1.5 billion for four transmission projects on October 3, 2024.
anchor: On October 3, 2024, the U.S. Department of Energy announced an investment of $1.5 billion in four transmission projects
locator: TFP selections page, opening paragraph; TFP FAQ
context: DOE pages as of November 2026 (second Trump administration) describing Biden-era selections. Selections are conditional until contracts are signed, and DOE obligates money only at signing.

submitted a notice to terminate the SWIP-N project capacity contract facilitation agreement with DOE effective June 30, 2026.

statement: On October 1, 2025 DOE announced the termination of 321 financial awards supporting 223 projects, approximately $7.56 billion, and said 26% of the awards were made between Election Day and Inauguration Day.

the termination of 321 financial awards supporting 223 projects, resulting in a savings of approximately $7.56 billion

The OBBBA barred reallocating credits revoked for noncompliance (CRS IN12624, saved elsewhere).

statement: The Joint Committee on Taxation, as cited by CRS, projects the 45X manufacturing credit will reduce federal revenues by $20.1 billion from FY2025 through FY2029, the fifth-highest projected five-year cost among 53 energy and natural resources tax expenditures studied.

context: CRS (nonpartisan) citing JCT (Congress's nonpartisan scorekeeper), December 2025 estimates; a projection of revenue loss, not a measure of results, and it falls after P.L. 119-21 phased out the wind component credit. statement: Rhodium Group's Clean Investment Monitor found annual clean-technology manufacturing investment declined 17% to $42 billion in 2025, and that $23 billion of manufacturing investment tied to 24 projects was canceled in 2025, against $6 billion in all earlier years.

statement: GSA announced in November 2023 a $2 billion investment for more than 150 construction projects using low-embodied-carbon asphalt, concrete, glass and steel, funded by the Inflation Reduction Act.

statement: UK Contracts for Difference generators paid back approximately £205 million into the scheme from September 2021 to March 2022 inclusive, according to a March 2022 ministerial answer, because market prices were above strike prices.

statement: Keyfacts Energy, using LCCC data, reports that UK CfD generators repaid a net £346m in 2022 and that the net cost of the scheme since inception is £12.2bn.

statement: Keyfacts Energy reports that UK CfD subsidies were a record £2.64bn in 2025, mostly to offshore wind, and that the average strike price for active offshore wind CfDs is over £150/MWh.
anchor: A record total of £2.64bn was paid out in subsidies across a range of technologies, but the largest recipient was offshore wind, taking over £2bn of the total.
the average strike price for active offshore wind CfDs is over £150/MWh.

context: Keyfacts Energy (UK trade news), January 2026, from LCCC data. Strike prices are indexed to inflation and set in different price years, so the £150/MWh average mixes price bases; subsidies per MWh depend on the market price, which is why they were negative in 2022.

statement: Germany's economy ministry announced on October 15, 2024 that 15 companies would receive a maximum of €2.8 billion in total in the first round of carbon contracts for difference, which have a 15-year term.
anchor: The 15 companies will receive a maximum of €2.8 billion in total
The carbon contracts for difference have a 15-year term.

statement: Reuters reported that the 15 first-round German carbon contract projects were expected to reduce emissions by 17 million metric tons over the contracts' 15-year term; the ministry's English release says 17 billion tonnes, which appears to be an error.
anchor: The 15 projects are expected to contribute to a reduction of 17 million metric tons of emissions over the contracts' 15-year term.

statement: ARD tagesschau quoted Economy Minister Robert Habeck in October 2024 as saying the first contracts lower emissions in the highly energy-intensive sector by 17 million tonnes, with total support of up to 2,8 Milliarden Euro.

indicating a cost "learning curve" of ~30% cost savings between Vogtle units 3 and 4.

statement: Lazard's July 2026 LCOE+ gives unsubsidized levelized cost ranges per megawatt-hour of $40 to $98 for utility-scale solar, $37 to $99 for onshore wind, $67 to $111 for geothermal and $105 to $167 for offshore wind.

statement: BloombergNEF's 2025 survey found lithium-ion battery pack prices dropped 8% since 2024 to a record low of $108 per kilowatt-hour, and stationary storage pack prices dropped to $70/kWh, 45% lower than in 2024.

statement: NLR's 2025 Annual Technology Baseline projects overnight capital cost reductions for a 60-MW 4-hour battery of 22% (Conservative), 45% (Moderate) and 66% (Advanced) between 2023 and 2035.

statement: NREL-lab researchers (2025) estimated that drilling costs for geothermal wells fell 12% to 24% for vertical wells and 18% to 26% for horizontal wells below the GeoVision baseline, and that drilling accounts for 30% to 57% of the cost to develop a plant.

drilling costs across the first four horizontal wells at Cape falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million per well.

other emergency orders issued since 2000, the grid operators in these cases had not requested the

statement: Census and university economists found that U.S. coal workers most exposed to the industry's decline lost earnings equal to 1.6 years of pre-decline wages, from 0.37 fewer years employed and 17 percent lower annual earnings in 2012-2019.

uniformly reduce economywide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 5-148 million metric tons annually in 2040 and as much as 1.5 gigatons cumulatively
context: Rhodium Group (see EV-CLP-743 for publisher, funding, date and model scope). Headline check: the bill savings combine the transmission provisions with the data-center cost-allocation provisions; Rhodium says the transmission mechanism drives 61%, 4% and 50% of the 2040 price decline in the low, mid and high scenarios, so in the mid case most of the saving comes from the ratepayer provisions. The 1.5 gigatons is the low-emissions scenario; the mid scenario is 368 million metric tons cumulative and the high scenario about 5 million a year in 2040. The figures also include gas pipeline provisions and LNG effects.

statement: Resources for the Future projected that the permitting bill's modeled provisions would raise overall transmission capacity about 30 percent above baseline by 2041, with interregional capacity more than doubling, and cut cumulative power-sector carbon dioxide emissions by about 1.8 gigatonnes through 2041.
anchor: we project overall transmission capacity to increase by 30 percent over the baseline; interregional transmission capacity more than doubles.
cumulative carbon dioxide emissions from the power sector declining by about 1.8 gigatonnes (Gt) through 2041 as compared to the baseline
context: Resources for the Future (nonpartisan research institution), issue brief by Kevin Rennert and Aaron Bergman, October 29, 2026; uses NREL's (now National Laboratory of the Rockies) ReEDS model with a high-demand scenario; models only power-sector effects of selected provisions, represents the permit-certainty sections as intended rather than as possibly broader, and uses 2024 technology costs without tariff increases. The text gives 1.83 gigatons in the emissions section. Power sector only to 2041, so it is not comparable with Rhodium's economy-wide 1.5 gigatons through 2040 (EV-CLP-744).

statement: FERC Commissioner David Rosner wrote in a concurrence in Docket No. ER26-1311-000, on Southwest Power Pool's interregional coordination tariff, that since 2011 Order No. 1000's interregional consultation requirements have resulted in exactly zero interregional transmission projects.
anchor: Since 2011, Order No. 1000’s interregional consultation requirements have resulted in exactly zero interregional transmission projects.
context: FERC (independent federal regulator) news page for Commissioner Rosner's concurrence; the page shows no date, and its docket link carries accession number 20260410, consistent with April 2026. One commissioner's statement, not a Commission finding, and he cites no list of projects. It supports the point that interregional planning under Order 1000 has produced no projects, a point CRS and others also make. Rosner is a Democratic appointee.

statement: Wood Mackenzie estimated that U.S. power transformers would face a supply shortage of 30% in 2025 (distribution transformers 10%), and that imports would account for about 80% of U.S. power transformer supply.
anchor: a supply shortage for power and distribution transformers to hit 30% and 10%, respectively, in 2025
In 2025, imports will account for an estimated 80% of US power transformer supply and 50% of the distribution transformer supply.
context: Wood Mackenzie (research and consultancy firm that sells market research), press release of August 14, 2025 on its report "Untangling the US transformer supply chain crisis". Mismatch with the request: the 128-week lead time is not in this press release; trade press (EEPower, POWER) attributes 128 weeks for power transformers (144 for step-up units) to Wood Mackenzie's second-quarter 2025 survey, so it is not recorded here. Wood Mackenzie's own August 13, 2025 commentary gives the distribution deficit as 6%, not 10%. POWER (January 2026) quotes a transformer maker who disputes that a shortage exists. McKinsey's separate estimate is EV-CLP-748.

statement: McKinsey estimated that in Europe and North America combined, power transformer demand of 914 GVA exceeded supply of 566 GVA by 38 percent in 2025.
anchor: In these markets, domestic power transformer demand of 914 GVA exceeded supply of 566 GVA by 38 percent in 2025.
locator: Section on the supply and demand gap
context: McKinsey & Company (consultancy), article "The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply" by Hirschberg, Reus and Schleyer, September 18, 2026; based on McKinsey Energy Solutions data and expert interviews, and McKinsey sells advice to utilities and manufacturers. The 38% covers Europe and North America together, not the United States alone, so it supports but is not the same measure as Wood Mackenzie's 30% for the U.S. (EV-CLP-747). It also reports lead times up to five years.

statement: Bonneville Power Administration described its Grid Expansion and Reinforcement Portfolio as a nearly $8 billion portfolio across 20+ major projects reinforcing the regional backbone to unlock roughly 10,000 MW of capacity.
anchor:
– Nearly $8 billion portfolio across 20+ major projects reinforcing the
regional backbone to unlock roughly 10,000 MW of capacity
context: BPA (DOE power marketing administration), October 2026 staff presentation (copy hosted on a Washington State site). A self-description of plans, not built capacity. Mismatch with the request: this slide does not say "mostly rebuilds and reconductoring". BPA's project summaries (not recorded as sources) put the first tranche at about $2 billion, "mostly upgrades, rebuilds and other improvements to existing facilities", and the second at $3.9 billion with new 500 kV lines among its projects, which sums to about $5.9 billion, not nearly $8 billion; the difference is unexplained. BPA borrowing authority is EV-CLP-420.

statement: Grid Strategies listed MISO's Tranche 2.1 portfolio at $21.8 billion with about 1,900 miles of 765 kV, SPP's 2025 plan at $8.6 billion with 949 miles of 765 kV, ERCOT's 765 kV plan at an estimated $20 billion for 2,468 miles, and PJM's investments since 2023 at over 1,100 miles of 500 kV, 765 kV and 525 kV HVDC lines for just over $10 billion.
anchor: MISO’s Long Range Transmission Plan Tranche 2.1 portfolio, approved by the MISO Board in December 2024, which is a $21.8 billion portfolio with approximately 1,900 miles of 765 kV transmission projects

context: Grid Strategies LLC, November 2026 (see EV-CLP-734 for funder and stance). A secondary roll-up of plans approved by regional operators, not funded or built lines; the report cites MISO, SPP, ERCOT, PUCT and PJM documents. Differences: the same firm's congestion report puts ERCOT's 765 kV backbone at nearly $33 billion (EV-CLP-753); PJM's total 2025 baseline approvals were $11.8 billion across all voltages (EV-CLP-752); a 2026 blog by an advocacy group for Texas 765 kV lines gives MISO's 765 kV mileage as roughly 1,800 (not recorded). MISO's own page confirms $21.8 billion, 24 projects and a 3,631-mile 765 kV backbone, in service 2032-2034 (not recorded as a source); SPP's press release confirms $8.6 billion (not recorded).

statement: PJM's Board approved 122 new baseline projects in the 2025 Regional Transmission Expansion Plan at an estimated cost of $11.8 billion, primarily to maintain system reliability.
anchor: PJM’s RTEP process identified 122 new baseline projects in 2025 at an estimated cost of $11.8 billion, primarily to maintain system reliability.
context: PJM Interconnection (regional grid operator for 13 states and D.C.), 2025 RTEP report. Costs are PJM's estimates; the spending is mostly local and regional reliability and load growth, not interregional lines, and the projects are paid for by PJM customers.

statement: Grid Strategies' congestion report said ERCOT and the Public Utility Commission of Texas approved a 765 kV backbone plan comprising several thousand new miles of transmission and nearly $33 billion in investment, not expected online until the early 2030s.
anchor: have also approved a significant 765 kV backbone transmission plan to serve, in part, oil and gas-related demand growth in the Permian Basin, comprising several thousand new miles of transmission and representing nearly $33 billion in investment.
While not expected to come online until the early 2030s
context: Grid Strategies LLC, September 2026, prepared for the Connected Grid Initiative (advocacy coalition); cites ERCOT's January 2025 comparison document, which was not obtained. The firm's November 2026 report gives ERCOT's STEP as an estimated $20 billion for 2,468 miles (EV-CLP-751); the two reports are not reconciled, possibly by plan scope. ERCOT is outside FERC backstop siting under both current law and the bill.

statement: The 2025 reconciliation law (P.L. 119-21), in its section 50402 on repeals and rescissions, rescinds the unobligated balances of amounts made available under Inflation Reduction Act sections 50151, 50152 and 50153, codified at 42 U.S.C. 18715, 18715a and 18715b.
anchor: SEC. 50402. REPEALS; RESCISSIONS.

(1) In general.--The unobligated balances of amounts made available under
the sections described in paragraph (2) are rescinded.
context: Primary law, enacted July 4, 2025 (OBBBA, P.L. 119-21), GPO enrolled text. The law gives no dollar amounts, so the unobligated balances rescinded are not stated; the request's "$2B unobligated" is unverified. CRS Insight IN11981 (not recorded as a source) describes the original appropriations as $2 billion for transmission facility financing loans (50151, for lines in designated corridors), $760 million for siting grants (50152) and $100 million for interregional and offshore wind transmission planning (50153). DOE's NIETC page lists the rescission of Transmission Facility Financing funding among its reasons for ending the corridor process (EV-CLP-737).

statement: EIA reported that the SunZia Wind Project in New Mexico (3,650 megawatts, with a 550-mile high voltage direct current transmission line) was slated to begin commercial operations that month, after Pattern Energy started construction in 2023 following almost two decades of permitting and planning.
anchor: The SunZia Wind Project, the largest wind farm in the United States, is slated to begin commercial operations this month.
has a total net summer generating capacity of 3,650 megawatts (MW)
Pattern Energy started construction of the SunZia Wind Project in 2023 , after almost two decades of permitting and planning.
Pattern Energy also built the SunZia Transmission Project—a 550-mile high voltage direct current transmission line
locator: "Today in Energy", first and second paragraphs
context: EIA (federal statistical agency), Today in Energy, June 12, 2026 (second Trump administration). Mismatches with the request: the sources do not say about 17 years to permit. EIA says "almost two decades of permitting and planning"; Vox (October 2026, not recorded) says the project was proposed in 2006 and did not break ground for 17 years, and quotes a former Interior deputy secretary arguing that financing hindered it more than permitting; Reuters (June 18, 2026, not recorded) says fully operational after nearly two decades of permitting and construction. WECC's 2026 progress report (not recorded) says the line was energized in 2025 and in testing through early 2026, so "energized 2026" is wrong by that account; commercial operation began in June 2026.

anchor: which reached commercial operation on May 13, 2026, making it eligible to deliver clean hydropower from Hydro-Québec in Canada to New York City.
339 miles of total transmission line, the longest fully buried line in North America

statement: On January 23, 2026 the Illinois Supreme Court reversed the appellate court and affirmed the Illinois Commerce Commission's grant of a certificate of public convenience and necessity to Grain Belt Express, holding that a showing of current and present financial capability was not a condition of the certificate, with one justice taking no part, and remanded the other challenges to the appellate court.
anchor: Filed | January 23, 2026
Appellate court judgment reversed.
Commission decision affirmed.
Cause remanded.
Proof of GBX’s current and present financial capability was not a condition precedent to the issuance of the CPCN.
JUSTICE HOLDER WHITE took no part in the consideration or decision of this case.
locator: Concerned Citizens & Property Owners v. Illinois Commerce Comm'n, 2026 IL 131026, caption, para. 33 and paras. 37-40
context: Illinois Supreme Court opinion by Justice O'Brien. The 6-0 vote in the request is from press reports (NPR Illinois, Engineering News-Record, January 23-26, 2026, not recorded); the opinion shows six justices taking part and one taking no part. The holding is narrow: it concerns only the financing condition under the state Public Utilities Act, and the court left the constitutional and other statutory challenges to the appellate court. The ruling resolved a state permit question; the line's federal permitting (a FAST-41 schedule with an estimated completion date of 01/18/2027 on the federal dashboard, read through a search extract and not recorded as a source) is separate. The DOE loan guarantee for the project was terminated in July 2025 (EV-CLP-435).

statement: Grid Strategies reported over 10,000 miles of 500 kV and above transmission projects planned and scheduled to come online by 2034, about 84% of them between 2030 and 2034, according to utility and RTO data.
anchor: Across the country, over 10,000 miles of 500 kV+ transmission projects have been planned and are scheduled to come online by 2034.

Planned and scheduled lines, not built ones; the same report notes that Boardman-to-Hemingway has taken some 20 years of development.
